item.title: Dict 1.0
item.description:
Dict 1.0 (build 14)

Two fixes in this build.

A quiet last phrase no longer gets cut off

Build 12 taught Dict to keep listening after you let go of the dictation key. It could still miss the end of a sentence if you trailed off quietly while releasing the key, because Dict mistook the soft ending for silence and stopped right away. Dict now judges only what it hears after you let go, and waits for a real pause before it stops. If you'd already finished talking, you won't notice a difference.

Color scheme tiles fit in Settings

The color scheme tiles in Settings could overlap each other. They're sized to fit now.

item.title: Dict 1.0
item.description:
Dict 1.0 (build 13)

Cloud cleanup with your own OpenRouter key (experimental)

Dict still transcribes everything on your Mac. Now you can hand the cleanup step (punctuation, capitals, and the Clean and Polished styles) to a cloud model instead of Apple Intelligence. In testing it handles corrections like "no wait, the newsletter" more reliably and writes cleaner paragraphs.

To try it, open Settings and find Cloud cleanup in General. Paste an API key from [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai) and save it. That's it: cloud cleanup turns on as soon as a key is saved.

  • The default model is Claude Haiku 5.5. It came out fastest of the good models we tried, at about a second per cleanup. You can type any other OpenRouter model ID into the Model field.
  • It costs very little. Use is billed to your OpenRouter account. A typical dictation costs about a hundredth of a cent. Settings shows a running total for this Mac, the cost of your last dictation, and what OpenRouter has billed your key so far.
  • It falls back on its own. If a request fails or you're offline, that dictation uses Apple Intelligence instead.
  • Your key stays in your Mac's Keychain. Remove it, or turn the toggle off, and cleanup goes back to running on your Mac.

With cloud cleanup on, your transcript and the names Dict reads from the field you're dictating into are sent to OpenRouter for each dictation. Your audio never leaves your Mac. The [privacy page](https://github.com/mattbirchler/Dict-releases/blob/main/PRIVACY.md) has the details.

item.title: Dict 1.0
item.description:
Dict 1.0 (build 12)

This build fixes three things that made dictation feel unreliable.

Your last words make it in

If you let go of the dictation key while you were still finishing a sentence, the end of it could go missing, sometimes several words. Dict now keeps listening after you let go until you've actually stopped talking, then inserts everything you said. If you'd already finished, nothing changes. If you were mid-sentence, the text shows up a moment later with nothing cut off.

Fewer stray question marks

In hands-free mode, Dict tidies up punctuation for you, and it had a habit of ending ordinary statements with a question mark ("I think we're in good shape?"). Now a question mark only appears when what you said reads like a question.

No extra space on empty lines in Obsidian

With "Add a space before dictation when needed" turned on, dictating onto a fresh line in Obsidian could start with a stray space. Dict now recognizes the start of a line there and leaves the space out.

item.title: Dict 1.0
item.description:
Dict 1.0 (build 11)

Light mode

Dict has always been dark. Now you can pick. Open Settings and look for Appearance in General:

  • Dark is the look you already have, and it stays the default.
  • Light gives the Dict window and the dictation panel a bright, clean look.
  • Match System switches between dark and light along with your Mac.

Light mode works with all five color schemes. The dictation panel turns white, and the dots light up in deeper versions of your scheme's colors so they're easy to see. Graphite switches to dark gray dots on white.

The change applies right away, including to the dictation panel, so you can try each option and see what you like.

item.title: Dict 1.0
item.description:
Dict 1.0 (build 10)

Long dictations come out cleaner in Verbatim

Verbatim is still instant when you hold the key. When you tap Space to go hands-free, which is usually when you're dictating something longer like an email or a blog post, Dict now tidies the text before it goes in:

  • Names get capitalized. People, places, companies, and products come out the way they're usually written, like "iPhone" and "YouTube".
  • Punctuation is smarter, including question marks when you ask something.
  • Ums and stumbles are removed. Filler sounds like "um" and "uh" go away, and so do words you tripped over and repeated, like "the the".

Your wording doesn't change. Dict checks the result word by word, and if anything other than capitals, punctuation, fillers, or repeats changed, it uses exactly what you said instead. Words like "like" and "you know" stay, and so do your own corrections.

Tidying uses the on-device Apple Intelligence model, so expect a short pause after a long hands-free dictation. Coding apps keep working the way they did.

item.title: Dict 1.0
item.description:
Dict 1.0 (build 9)

Numbers come out as numbers

Say "twenty five" and you get 25. Dict used to write most numbers out in words, and this build fixes that in every dictation style, including Verbatim.

  • Everyday numbers: "three point five" becomes 3.5, "fifteen thousand" becomes 15,000, "three million" stays readable as 3 million.
  • Dates and times: "nineteen eighty four" becomes 1984, "the twenty first" becomes the 21st, and "meet at three thirty" becomes 3:30.
  • Numbers read one digit at a time join up, so a phone number or zip code comes out as one number.

Dict still leaves words alone when they aren't really counts. "This one" and "one of them" keep their "one", and "the first thing" stays the first thing.

item.title: Dict 1.0
item.description:
Dict 1.0 (build 8)

AirPods work properly now

If you dictate with AirPods, or switch between AirPods and another microphone, this build is for you.

  • No more crashes when you change mics. Taking AirPods out and dictating with your Mac's built-in mic or a USB mic used to crash Dict on the next keypress. Dict now reads the microphone's current format every time it starts recording instead of trusting what it saw last time, which is what the crash came down to.
  • The waveform appears right away. Bluetooth mics take about a second to switch on, and Dict used to wait for that before showing anything. Now the HUD comes up immediately and says CONNECTING until your AirPods are actually listening.
  • Recordings don't go silent. When a mic changes its settings mid-sentence, Dict picks the recording back up within a fraction of a second instead of recording silence until you let go.

Other microphones get the same treatment, so plugging one in or unplugging it between dictations is safe too.

item.title: Dict 1.0
item.description:
Dict 1.0 (build 7)

Insert a dictation again from the menu bar

Dictated while the wrong field was focused? Click into the right one, open the Dict menu, and choose Insert Last Dictation. The text goes in with the same spacing a new dictation would get.

  • Recent Dictations lists your last five, so you can put any of them back without opening History. Show All opens the full list.
  • Hold Option while the menu is open to copy instead of insert.

Anonymous usage data

Dict now sends a few anonymous counts, like how many words a dictation had and which engine you use. They show how much Dict gets used and where people get stuck setting it up.

  • Never sent: your audio, your words, your history, your word replacements, or your license key. Your IP address and location aren't stored either.
  • Turn it off in Settings, General, Share anonymous usage data. Nothing is sent after that.

The full list of what's sent is in the [privacy statement](https://github.com/mattbirchler/Dict-releases/blob/main/PRIVACY.md).

item.title: Dict 1.0
item.description:
Dict 1.0 (build 6)

Dict is now a paid app

Dict costs $9.99, once. There's no subscription and no account, and one purchase covers all of your Macs.

  • 14 days to try it. Your free trial starts the first time you open this version, and every feature works during it. The menu bar menu shows how many days are left.
  • When the trial ends, dictation stops until you enter a license key. Your settings, word replacements and history all stay where they are.
  • Buying takes a minute. Choose Buy Dict in the menu bar menu or in Settings under License. Checkout opens in your browser at dictapp.app. When it's done, click Activate in Dict on the confirmation page and Dict unlocks.
  • Your key stays on your Mac. Dict checks the key against a public key built into the app. It never sends your key anywhere or asks a server whether it's valid, so Dict still never goes online except to check for updates and to download the Parakeet model if you choose it.
  • Setting up another Mac? Settings, License has Copy License Key. Paste the key into Dict on the other Mac, or choose Enter License Key in the menu.

Thank you for trying Dict while it was free. If you have questions about the change, email matt@birchtree.me.

item.title: Dict 1.0
item.description:
Dict 1.0 (build 5)

Fixes

  • AirPods work as a microphone. Choosing AirPods recorded nothing, and the app could crash on your next key press. AirPods switch to a different audio format when their mic turns on, and Dict now follows that change instead of tripping over it. If a mic changes format mid-recording, Dict picks the recording back up.

Improvements

  • You can see when the speech model is loading. Right after launch, Parakeet takes a moment to load. The menu bar icon now animates while that happens, and the menu says "Loading speech model…". When it finishes, a short "Ready to dictate" notice appears at the bottom of the screen so you know you can start talking.
  • Names come out the way your document spells them, with any engine. Dict reads the field you're typing into and fixes names and terms to match it. "birchtree" becomes "Birchtree", "iphone" becomes "iPhone", and a name heard as two words ("birch tree") is joined back up. Before, this only worked when Apple Intelligence formatting ran, which with Parakeet was mostly in coding apps. Ordinary words are left alone, so a document that mentions "Mark" won't capitalize every "mark". You can turn this off in Settings under "Spell names the way the document does".

item.title: Dict 1.0
item.description:
Dict 1.0

The first public release. Dict is a menu bar dictation app for macOS 26 that runs entirely on your Mac: no account, no server, no subscription. Hold a key, talk, let go, and the words land where your cursor is.

What you get

  • Two on-device engines. Apple's speech engine works the moment you install. Download NVIDIA Parakeet from Settings for better accuracy on names, technical terms and long sentences. Dict switches over by itself when the download finishes.
  • Your key. Right Command, Right Option, Right Control, Fn, or any combination you record in Settings.
  • Hands-free. Tap Space while holding the key and Dict keeps listening until you press Command to finish or Escape to cancel. The panel grows to show the words as they arrive.
  • Dictation styles. Verbatim keeps every word. Clean drops ums, uhs and repeated words, and keeps only your corrected version when you change your mind mid-sentence. Polished adds small grammar fixes. Clean and Polished use Apple Intelligence on your Mac, so nothing leaves it.
  • Screen context. Dict reads the field you are typing into and spells names, acronyms and identifiers the way they already appear there. You can turn this off in Settings.
  • Word replacements. Teach Dict how to spell the words it keeps getting wrong.
  • History and stats. Every dictation is saved on your Mac with a limit you set, with words dictated, time saved and your day streak at the top.
  • Five color schemes: Ember, Phosphor, Glacier, Ultraviolet and Graphite. The scheme you pick lights up the dictation panel and the app's dark windows alike.

Privacy

Audio, transcripts, history and the text Dict reads from your screen never leave your Mac. The only network requests Dict makes are checking GitHub for updates and, if you ask for it, downloading the Parakeet model from Hugging Face. The privacy statement is in the About window.

Requirements

macOS 26 or later on Apple silicon. Dict asks for Microphone access to hear you and Accessibility access to type for you, and explains both the first time it runs.
